params.question: A patient presents after a blow to the side of the skull with bleeding from the right ear, conductive hearing loss, and no facial weakness. Two days later, mild facial asymmetry develops. What is the most likely fracture type and expected outcome?

answers.text: Transverse fracture — conductive hearing loss and delayed facial palsy are typical features of this pattern

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Transverse fractures result from anteroposterior blows and cause sensorineural hearing loss with immediate, severe facial palsy — the opposite of this presentation.

answers.text: Longitudinal fracture — delayed onset indicates progressive nerve compression with a poor prognosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In longitudinal fractures, delayed facial palsy indicates neuropraxia (a temporary conduction block), not progressive compression. The prognosis is good.

answers.text: Longitudinal fracture — the delayed, incomplete palsy reflects neuropraxia with a good prognosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A lateral blow causes a longitudinal fracture running through the middle ear (hence conductive loss). Delayed, incomplete facial palsy indicates neuropraxia — a temporary conduction block — and recovery is expected without surgery.

answers.text: Transverse fracture — the delayed palsy indicates nerve transection requiring urgent surgical decompression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Transverse fractures cause immediate complete palsy and sensorineural hearing loss after anteroposterior blows. Delayed onset points to neuropraxia from a longitudinal fracture.

overallFeedback.feedback: A lateral blow causes a longitudinal fracture through the middle ear (conductive loss). Delayed, incomplete facial palsy is neuropraxia — a temporary conduction block with good recovery. Transverse fractures from anteroposterior blows cause sensorineural loss and immediate palsy.

Well done. Longitudinal fractures from lateral blows pass through the middle ear, causing conductive hearing loss. Delayed facial palsy indicates neuropraxia with a favourable prognosis, whereas transverse fractures cause immediate, severe palsy.

params.question: A 28-year-old man with an untreated lower molar infection develops a brawny, board-like swelling of the floor of the mouth, with the tongue pushed upward. Which anatomical pathway explains how this infection can reach the mediastinum within hours?

answers.text: Direct extension through the hyoglossus muscle into the superior mediastinum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Infection does not spread through muscle tissue directly to the mediastinum. The fascial planes provide the actual pathway for rapid contiguous spread.

answers.text: Spread through the danger space, which lies between the alar and prevertebral fascia and extends from the skull base to the diaphragm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The danger space runs continuously between the alar fascia and prevertebral fascia, from the skull base to the diaphragm. Infection tracks along this uninterrupted corridor, potentially causing life-threatening mediastinitis within hours.

answers.text: Lymphatic drainage from the submandibular space into the mediastinal lymph nodes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lymphatic spread is far too slow to explain the rapid progression seen in deep neck infections. Contiguous fascial plane spread is the mechanism.

answers.text: Haematogenous spread via the internal jugular vein into the thorax

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Haematogenous spread would cause systemic septicaemia rather than the contiguous soft-tissue infection that characterises mediastinitis from deep neck infections.

overallFeedback.feedback: The danger space lies between the alar fascia and prevertebral fascia and extends continuously from the skull base to the diaphragm. This is why deep neck infections — often starting from a dental source — can cause life-threatening mediastinitis within hours.

Excellent. The danger space between the alar and prevertebral fascia is an uninterrupted corridor from the skull base to the diaphragm, allowing rapid contiguous spread of infection to the mediastinum.

interactions.label: A 45-year-old woman has a slow-growing, painless parotid mass confirmed as a ple

params.question: A 45-year-old woman has a slow-growing, painless parotid mass confirmed as a pleomorphic adenoma on fine-needle aspiration cytology. Why is enucleation contraindicated as the definitive surgical treatment?

answers.text: Enucleation carries an unacceptable risk of facial nerve injury during dissection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Facial nerve injury risk is actually managed by careful identification and preservation during formal parotidectomy. The concern with enucleation is incomplete tumour removal, not nerve risk.

answers.text: The tumour's deep-lobe extension makes complete enucleation technically impossible in most cases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Deep-lobe extension is not the primary concern. Even superficially located pleomorphic adenomas should not be enucleated, because of their characteristic growth pattern.

answers.text: Enucleation does not provide adequate tissue margins for histopathological staging of the tumour

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While adequate margins are important, the specific reason enucleation fails is the tumour's pseudopod projections that extend beyond the apparent capsule and seed recurrence.

answers.text: Pleomorphic adenomas have pseudopod projections beyond the visible capsule, making enucleation prone to multifocal recurrence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pleomorphic adenomas extend microscopic pseudopods beyond their apparent capsule. Enucleation leaves these behind, causing multifocal recurrence. Superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve identification and preservation is the standard procedure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Pleomorphic adenomas extend microscopic pseudopods beyond their visible capsule. Enucleation leaves these behind, causing multifocal recurrence. The standard operation is superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve identification and preservation — never enucleation, and never incisional biopsy.

Well done. Pseudopod projections beyond the apparent capsule mean that enucleation leaves residual tumour, leading to multifocal recurrence. The correct operation is superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation.

params.question: Oral hairy leukoplakia can be found in immunocompetent individuals and does not require HIV testing.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Oral hairy leukoplakia is pathognomonic of significant immunosuppression — it is never found in immunocompetent individuals. Finding it in a patient of unknown HIV status is an absolute indication for testing. Unlike oral candidiasis, it cannot be dismissed as an incidental finding.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Oral hairy leukoplakia is pathognomonic of significant immunosuppression and is never found in immunocompetent individuals. Its presence is an absolute indication for HIV testing, unlike oral candidiasis, which can occur without immunodeficiency.

interactions.label: A motorcyclist arrives after a road traffic accident with stridor, subcutaneous

params.question: A motorcyclist arrives after a road traffic accident with stridor, subcutaneous emphysema of the neck, a bilateral boggy swelling over the nasal septum, and Battle's sign behind the right ear. The ATLS primary survey is in progress. Which finding demands the FIRST site-specific ENT intervention?

answers.text: Stridor with subcutaneous emphysema — secure the airway, as this indicates a laryngeal fracture threatening complete airway loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Stridor with subcutaneous emphysema after neck trauma indicates a laryngeal fracture that can progress to complete airway obstruction. Securing the airway — often by tracheostomy — is the first priority. The septal haematoma has a 24–48 hour window, and temporal bone imaging can wait until the patient is stable.

answers.text: Battle's sign — arrange urgent HRCT temporal bone to rule out a transverse fracture

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Battle's sign indicates a temporal bone fracture but is not immediately life-threatening. Imaging is important but follows stabilisation of the airway.

answers.text: Septal haematoma — drain immediately to prevent saddle-nose deformity within 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Septal haematoma drainage is time-sensitive (within 24–48 hours), but a compromised airway is an immediate threat to life. The ATLS hierarchy places airway above all other interventions.

answers.text: Request contrast-enhanced CT of the neck before any intervention to guide surgical planning

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Imaging must never delay securing a compromised airway. A patient with stridor and subcutaneous emphysema can lose the airway while waiting for a scan. Secure first, image second.

overallFeedback.feedback: In the ATLS framework, airway always comes first. Stridor with subcutaneous emphysema after neck trauma indicates a laryngeal fracture threatening complete airway loss. Secure the airway first — often by tracheostomy. Then drain the septal haematoma (24–48 hour window) and arrange temporal bone imaging.

Well done. The ATLS hierarchy places airway first. Stridor with subcutaneous emphysema signals a laryngeal fracture that can progress to complete obstruction. Secure the airway, then address the septal haematoma (24–48 hour window), then image the temporal bone.
